content: Flax, also known as Common Flax or Linseed, belongs to the genus Linum in the family Linaceae. It is unrelated to New Zealand flax. This plant is native to a region stretching from the eastern Mediterranean to India and was likely first domesticated in the Fertile Crescent. Flax was widely cultivated in ancient Egypt. It is an annual plant that grows upright, reaching a height of 1 to 2 meters, with slender stems. The leaves are glaucous green, narrow, and lance-shaped, measuring 20-40 mm in length and 3 mm in width. The flowers are pale blue, with a diameter of 15-25 mm, and consist of five petals. The fruit is a small, round, dry capsule, 5-9 mm in diameter, containing several glossy brown seeds shaped like apple pips, each 4-7 mm long. The term flax can also refer to the unspun fibers derived from the plant. Flax is cultivated for both its seeds and fibers. Different parts of the plant have been historically used to produce fabric, dye, paper, medicines, fishing nets, and soap. It is also grown as an ornamental plant due to its ability to produce true blue flowers, a rarity among plants. However, not all flax varieties produce blue flowers. Flax Seeds Flax seeds yield a vegetable oil known as linseed oil or flaxseed oil, one of the oldest commercial oils. Solvent-processed flaxseed oil has been used for centuries as a drying oil in painting and varnishing. Flax seeds are available in two main varieties: brown and yellow (golden). Both types have similar nutritional profiles and contain comparable amounts of short-chain omega-3 fatty acids. However, a specific yellow variety called solin (or Linola) is low in omega-3 and has a distinct oil composition. A newer yellow flax variety, Omega, developed by North Dakota State University, was created primarily for food consumption. This variety has a nutty-buttery flavor and contains omega-3 fatty acids at levels comparable to brown flax. Ground flax seeds can serve as an egg substitute in baking, with one tablespoon of ground flax seeds mixed with three tablespoons of water replacing one egg. They can also be added to oatmeal, yogurt, or other foods to impart a nutty flavor. Flaxseed oil is commonly consumed in salads or as capsules. The nutritional benefits of flax seeds are attributed to lignans and omega-3 essential fatty acids. Flaxseed oil is also sometimes recommended as a galactagogue to promote lactation. However, excessive consumption of flax seeds can lead to diarrhea. Lignans, another component of flax seeds, have heart-protective and anti-cancer properties. Research led by Lilian U. Thompson at the University of Toronto has shown that flaxseed can reduce tumor growth in mice, particularly in postmenopausal breast cancer. These effects are believed to be due to lignans and are additive when combined with tamoxifen. Preliminary studies suggest similar benefits in human cancer patients. There is also some evidence that flaxseed may be beneficial in other cancers, such as prostate cancer. Additionally, flax may help stabilize blood sugar levels, potentially reducing the severity of diabetes. Flax seed sprouts are edible and have a slightly spicy flavor. Flax seeds are known by various names in different languages, such as San or Alsi in Hindi, Gujarati, and Punjabi, Ali Vidai in Tamil, Jawas or Alashi in Marathi, Tishi in Bengali, Pesi in Oriya, Agasi in Kannada, Avise ginzalu in Telugu, and Cheruchana vithu in Malayalam. Flax Fibers Flax fibers are among the oldest fiber crops in the world. The use of flax for linen production dates back 5,000 years. Ancient Egyptian tombs and temple walls in Thebes depict flowering flax plants. In northern Europe, flax fiber was used for cloth production during the Neolithic period. In North America, flax was introduced by the Puritans. Today, most flax grown in the USA and Canada is cultivated for seed production, either for linseed oil or for human nutrition. Flax fiber is extracted from the bast, or outer skin, of the plant's stem. It is soft, lustrous, and flexible, with greater strength than cotton but less elasticity. High-quality flax fibers are used to produce linen fabrics such as damasks, lace, and sheeting, while coarser fibers are used for twine and rope. Flax fiber is also a raw material for high-quality paper, including banknotes and cigarette rolling paper. Flax Mills The first flax mills for spinning flaxen yarn were invented in 1787 by John Kendrew and Thomas Porthouse of Darlington. Cultivation Major flax-producing countries include Canada, the USA, and China, with significant production also occurring in India and Europe. Flax thrives in deep, friable loams rich in organic matter. Heavy clay soils and dry, sandy soils are unsuitable. Flax farming requires minimal fertilizers and pesticides. Within six weeks of sowing, the plant reaches a height of 10-15 cm and grows several centimeters per day under optimal conditions, reaching 70-80 cm within 15 days. Flax for fiber production is harvested approximately 100 days after sowing, about a month after flowering and two weeks after seed capsule formation. The plant's base turns yellow when ready for harvest. If harvested too early, the seeds will be underdeveloped, and the fibers will be of poor quality. The mature plant is pulled up with its roots intact to maximize fiber length. After drying, the seeds are removed, and the plant undergoes retting, a process that separates the fibers from the stalk. Retting can take 2 weeks to 2 months, depending on climatic conditions and the characteristics of the flax and fields. During retting, enzymatic action breaks down the pectins binding the fibers to the straw. Once retted and dried, the flax is rolled up and stored before scutching to extract the fibers. Flax grown for seed is allowed to mature until the seed capsules turn yellow and begin to split. It is then harvested using a combine harvester and dried to extract the seeds. Threshing Flax Threshing involves removing seeds from the rest of the plant. The process has two stages. The first stage, performed by the farmer, prepares the flax for general use. This involves three machines: one for threshing the seeds, one for breaking and separating the woody parts from the fibers, and one for further refining the fibers. In some cases, farmers thresh the seeds in their own mills, eliminating the need for the first machine. The second stage, performed by manufacturers, prepares the flax for fine purposes such as lace, cambric, damask, and fine linen. This stage uses a refining machine. Preparation for Spinning Before flax fibers can be spun into linen, they must be separated from the stalk. The first step, retting, involves rotting away the inner stalk to leave the outer fibers intact. The remaining straw is then broken into small pieces, scraped away during scutching, and combed out using hackles. Retting Flax Retting can be done in ponds, streams, fields, or containers. Pond retting is the fastest method, taking a few days to a couple of weeks, but it can result in lower-quality fibers and produces a strong odor. Stream retting takes longer (2-3 weeks) but yields cleaner fibers with less odor. Field retting, which involves laying flax in a field to collect dew, takes over a month but produces the highest-quality fibers and minimal pollution. Retting can also be done in watertight containers, with the process taking 4-5 days at 80°F. Lower temperatures extend the process. This method produces scum and odor similar to pond retting. Dressing the Flax Dressing flax involves breaking, scutching, and hackling to remove straw from the fibers. Breaking crushes the straw, scutching scrapes it away, and hackling combs out the remaining bits. Symbolism Common flax is the national flower of Belarus and serves as the emblem of the Northern Ireland Assembly. The flax plant, depicted in a coronet, appeared on the reverse of British one-pound coins minted in 1986 and 1991. Popular Culture In English, blond hair is traditionally described as fair or flaxen.
